title: MATH GAOKAO - 21
description: Authentic-style mathematics problems inspired by China’s Gaokao — build deeper understanding, sharper thinking, and real exam readiness.

questions.concept: Subset Relation as a Logical Implication
questions.learningObjective: Identify the logical statement equivalent to \(A\subseteq B\).
questions.question: Which statement is equivalent to \(A\subseteq B\)?
questions.explanation:
By definition, \(A\subseteq B\) means every element of \(A\) is also an element of \(B\). In logical notation, this is written as
\[
\forall x,\ (x\in A \rightarrow x\in B).
\]
Option A uses disjunction instead of implication, so it is not the correct translation.
questions.hint: Recall the definition of a subset in terms of elements.

questions.question: What is the negation of \(A\subseteq B\)?
questions.explanation:
The statement \(A\subseteq B\) is
\[
\forall x,\ (x\in A \rightarrow x\in B).
\]
Its negation is
\[
\exists x,\ \neg(x\in A \rightarrow x\in B).
\]
Since \(\neg(P\rightarrow Q)\equiv P\land\neg Q\), this becomes
\[
\exists x,\ (x\in A \land x\notin B).
\]
Therefore, the negation is option B.
questions.hint: Negate the universal statement and then negate the implication.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the intersection and union of two finite sets.
questions.question: Let \(U=\{1,2,3,4\}\), \(A=\{1,2\}\), and \(B=\{2,3\}\). Which statement is true?
questions.explanation:
The intersection \(A\cap B\) consists of elements common to both sets. The only common element is \(2\), so
\[
A\cap B=\{2\}.
\]
The union \(A\cup B\) is
\[
A\cup B=\{1,2\}\cup\{2,3\}=\{1,2,3\},
\]
which is not equal to \(\{1,2,3,4\}\). Therefore, option A is true and option B is false.
questions.hint: Find the common elements for the intersection, and combine all elements for the union.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the logical equivalence corresponding to \((A\cup B)^c=A^c\cap B^c\).
questions.question: Which logical equivalence corresponds to the set identity \((A\cup B)^c=A^c\cap B^c\)?

options.label: A
options.text:
\(
eg(x\in A \lor x\in B)\equiv(x
otin A \land x
otin B)\)

options.label: B
options.text:
\(
eg(x\in A \land x\in B)\equiv(x
otin A \lor x
otin B)\)

questions.explanation:
The statement \(x\in (A\cup B)^c\) is equivalent to
\[
\neg(x\in A \lor x\in B).
\]
By De Morgan's law for logic,
\[
\neg(x\in A \lor x\in B)\equiv(x\notin A \land x\notin B).
\]
Thus option A correctly expresses the set identity. Option B corresponds to the complement of an intersection, not a union.
questions.hint: Use De Morgan's law to negate a disjunction.

questions.concept: Negation of an Existential Set Statement
questions.learningObjective: Negate the statement \(\exists x,\ (x\in A \land x\notin B)\).
questions.question: What is the negation of \(\exists x,\ (x\in A \land x\notin B)\)?
questions.explanation:
The negation of an existential statement is universal. We have
\[
\neg\bigl(\exists x,\ (x\in A \land x\notin B)\bigr)
\equiv
\forall x,\ \neg(x\in A \land x\notin B).
\]
By De Morgan's law,
\[
\neg(x\in A \land x\notin B)\equiv(x\notin A \lor x\in B).
\]
This is logically equivalent to
\[
\forall x,\ (x\in A \rightarrow x\in B).
\]
Therefore, the negation is option B.
questions.hint: Negate the existential quantifier, then simplify the inner statement.

questions.learningObjective: Determine which subset relations hold among given finite sets.
questions.question: Let \(A=\{1,2\}\), \(B=\{2,3\}\), and \(C=\{1,2,3\}\). Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: Check the elements of \(A=\{1,2\}\). Both \(1\) and \(2\) belong to \(C=\{1,2,3\}\), so \(A\subseteq C\). Similarly, both elements of \(B=\{2,3\}\) belong to \(C\), so \(B\subseteq C\). Thus option A is true. For option B, \(A\subseteq B\) is false because \(1\in A\) but \(1\notin B\). Also \(B\subseteq A\) is false because \(3\in B\) but \(3\notin A\). Therefore, option B is false.
questions.hint: Check every element of each set against the proposed superset.

questions.learningObjective: Determine which set equality necessarily follows from \(A\subseteq B\).
questions.question: If \(A\subseteq B\), which statement is necessarily true?
questions.explanation:
Since \(A\subseteq B\), every element of \(A\) is also an element of \(B\). Therefore, the common elements of \(A\) and \(B\) are exactly the elements of \(A\), so
\[
A\cap B=A.
\]
The union \(A\cup B\) is actually \(B\), not \(A\), unless \(A=B\). Hence option B is not necessarily true.
questions.hint: Use the definition of subset to determine what happens to intersection and union.

questions.question: Which condition is equivalent to \(A=B\)?
questions.explanation:
Two sets are equal exactly when they contain the same elements. This happens if and only if each is a subset of the other:
\[
A=B \iff (A\subseteq B \land B\subseteq A).
\]
Option A only states one direction, so it is not sufficient for equality.
questions.hint: Recall that equality of sets requires mutual containment.

questions.concept: Negation of a Universal Set Statement
questions.learningObjective: Negate the statement \(\forall x,\ (x\in A \rightarrow P(x))\).
questions.question: What is the negation of \(\forall x,\ (x\in A \rightarrow P(x))\)?
questions.explanation:
The negation of a universal statement is existential:
\[
\neg\bigl(\forall x,\ (x\in A \rightarrow P(x))\bigr)
\equiv
\exists x,\ \neg(x\in A \rightarrow P(x)).
\]
Since \(\neg(P\rightarrow Q)\equiv P\land\neg Q\), we get
\[
\exists x,\ (x\in A \land \neg P(x)).
\]
Therefore, the negation is option A. Option B is not the negation; it is logically equivalent to the original statement.
questions.hint: Negate the universal quantifier and then negate the implication.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the logical statement equivalent to \(A\cap B=\varnothing\).
questions.question: Which statement is equivalent to \(A\cap B=\varnothing\)?
questions.explanation:
The statement \(A\cap B=\varnothing\) means that no element belongs to both \(A\) and \(B\). In logical form, this is
\[
\forall x,\ \neg(x\in A \land x\in B).
\]
By De Morgan's law,
\[
\neg(x\in A \land x\in B)\equiv(x\notin A \lor x\notin B).
\]
Therefore,
\[
A\cap B=\varnothing \iff \forall x,\ (x\notin A \lor x\notin B).
\]
Option A says every element of \(A\) is in \(B\), which means \(A\subseteq B\), not disjointness.
questions.hint: Translate “no element is in both sets” and apply De Morgan's law.
